item.title: Cumulative risk, center-based childcare and socio-emotional difficulties in early childhood: Evidence from Hungary (by Zsuzsanna Veroszta, Krisztina Kopcsó, Zsolt Spéder)
item.description: Background: Although center-based childcare attendance under age 3 is widespread in Europe, there is mixed evidence on its impact on children’s socio-emotional well-being. item.title: “Family-Anchored” transitions to adult life in Mexico (by Federica Becca, Albert Esteve)
item.description: Background: It is common for young adults in Mexico to coreside with own parents or other extended family members when forming the first partnership or becoming a parent/single parent. This practice has scarcely been studied in the literature and yet plays a very relevant role in understanding transitions to adulthood in the Latin American context. item.title: Tracking the decline of first marriage in South Korea: Timing, quantum decline, and pandemic disruptions (by Sam Hyun Yoo)
item.description: Background: In South Korea, where most births occur within marriage, the country’s record-low fertility has put renewed attention on the long-term decline in first marriage. Despite rising policy and academic interest, systematic demographic analyses that disentangle structural and timing components of nuptiality change remain limited, especially in East Asia. item.title: Local dialect proficiency and migrants’ identity integration: A case of Shanghai (by Simin Zhang, Muzhi Zhou)
item.description: Background: Language proficiency is a crucial factor in migrant integration; however, few studies have examined the relationship between local dialect acquisition and migrant integration in China, a country with numerous dialects. The significance of dialects in shaping regional identity, nonetheless, may have diminished as Putonghua becomes increasingly popular. item.title: The demography of loneliness: Rethinking social connections in population research (by Hisrael Passarelli-Araujo)
item.description: Background: Loneliness is often treated as an individual or psychological experience, but it also reflects broader demographic and structural shifts. Population aging, declining fertility, migration, and shifting household arrangements have reshaped the ways individuals connect, care, and live. Despite its growing social relevance, loneliness remains under-theorized and under-measured in demographic research. item.description: Background: Estimating infertility prevalence at the population level is challenging and little is known about the factors that influence how individuals report it. item.description: Background: Understanding the relationship between early learning and later fertility preferences and knowledge could yield important lessons for public policy in both the education and health sectors.
